# dsh-batch-triage

**Rules decide the easy tickets. Anything the rules cannot place is handed to a
human — never quietl
y filed as routine.**

A DeepSeek Harness plugin.
No model, no service, no network, no API key.
[代码示例省略，未执行]
## Why rules first

A ticket batch is the wrong shape for one model call per item: the volume is high,
the interesting i

tems are few, and every item costs a round trip whether or not it
needed one. So the order is invert
ed from the obvious one.

**The prefilter runs on every item, first.** Rules place the clear cases — a crash
with a stack trac

e is urgent, "how do I install this" is routine — and they place
them without asking anything. Only

the residue would ever reach a model, and this
release does not reach one at all: it says so instead

he residue would ever reach a model, and this
release does not reach one at all: it says so instead.

That ordering is not an optimisation. It is the design's main path, and it changes
what the tool is
for: **the prefilter is the product, and the model is a fallback.**
## What the rules look at

A **structured field outranks the body text**: `severity: critical`,
`security: true`, `data_loss: t

rue`, `reporter_tier: enterprise`. A reporter who
filled in a form has already told you, and no word

ing in the body can lower what the
field said. Wording that reports something *worse* still raises i

t — a field can never
bury an outage, and when the two disagree the item carries both reason codes.

Otherwise **the highest class any rule claims wins**, and the table is written
strongest first so th
at a tie inside a class goes to the rule listed first:
| class | rules |

| `urgent` | `outage`, `data_loss`, `security`, `crash_with_trace`, `blocked_workflow` |
| `needs_re

view` | `regression`, `wrong_result`, `performance`, `flaky` |
| `routine` | `install_question`, `us
age_question`, `documentation`, `feature_request`, `thanks` |

A ticket that reports an outage *and* phrases itself as a question must not be
swallowed by the ques

tion rule. That is a test — and in 0.1.1 it was a test that could
not fail, because its fixture used

wording the `outage` rule already recognised, so the
fixture and the rule shared an assumption and

the precedence was never really exercised.
Precedence is by class rather than by position now, which

also means a caller-supplied
`rules` array cannot reorder the table into a fail-open.

Class precedence alone was not enough, and the six measured tickets below are why.
`outage` did not

know "returns 500 for every request", so *no* severity rule matched,
and the question rule decided t

he whole ticket from one sentence of it. So a `routine`
verdict gets one more check: if the body rep

orts a malfunction — an error, a crash,
something "unusable", a 5xx, deleted records, a leaked crede

ntial — in wording no
severity rule could name, the item becomes `needs_review` with `MALFUNCTION_RE

PORTED`
instead of `routine`. That guard only ever *refuses* a `routine`; it cannot raise
anything t
o `urgent`, and it cannot touch a verdict a severity rule already made.

Precedence by class is chosen over "most specific wins" deliberately. A scoring system

## What `failOn` does
`failOn` decides which classes count as a finding (exit `1`):
| value | a finding is… |

| `any` (default) | an urgent item, any escalation, **or any `needs_review`** |
| `urgent` | an urge

nt item only |
| `none` | nothing — the caller asked for a report, not a gate |

A `needs_review` is a "a human should look" decision whether it came from a
prefilter rule (`regress

ion`, `wrong_result`, `performance`, `flaky`, field
`severity: high|medium`) or from a residual (`no

rule matched`, model unavailable,
budget exhausted). Before 0.1.3 only residual items counted, so a

batch containing a
single regression ticket exited `0 clean` even though a rule had already said it

needs a human. That gap is closed: under `any`, a rule-decided `needs_review` is a
finding.

Exit codes still outrank findings. A residual item with no model client exits `6`
(`modelUnavailable

`) before the finding rung, and a usage/config error outranks
both. So the shipped plugin has two vi

e finding rung, and a usage/config error outranks
both. So the shipped plugin has two visible cases:
| batch | effect of `failOn` |

| contains a residual item (no rule matched) | exits `6` regardless of `failOn` |
| every item was d
ecided, at least one as `needs_review` | `any` → `1`; `urgent` / `none` → `0` |

`modelClient` is a library-level option and is deliberately not part of the YAML
config block below:

it is a seam for tests and for a host that supplies a client
programmatically. It is still never ca

lled in this release — `modelClass` stays
`unavailable`.
## What `tau` can and cannot do here

`tau` is the escalation threshold on confidence, and this release has no confidence
to compare again

st. So it does the one thing the design permits: it can make a
`needs_review` item escalate, and it

**never downgrades anything**. An option that
was accepted and had no effect would be worse than one

that is rejected, because
the caller would believe something had been checked.
## What the rules do with a severity they do not recognise

An unrecognised `severity` — `P4`, `banana`, `kritisch` — is **not** treated as an
absent one. Dropp

ing it is how a real priority silently becomes `routine`, and
raising it to urgent would invent a si

gnal. So it becomes `needs_review` with
`FIELD_SEVERITY_UNRECOGNISED`: the field said something abou

t priority and this
release does not know what, which is a question rather than a guess in either
di

ty and this
release does not know what, which is a question rather than a guess in either
direction.

The recognised vocabulary is wide on purpose (`critical`, `blocker`, `sev1`, `s1`,
`P0`, `urgent`, `

emergency`, `showstopper`, `severity 1`, `1`, `highest` for the top
tier), because 0.1.0 accepted fo

ur labels and `severity: 'P0'` then behaved exactly
like no severity at all.
## Requirements

Node `^22.19.0 || >=24.0.0`. No runtime dependencies. `@deepseek-ai/cordis` is an
optional peer.
